assertion: The state of New York received a 'C-' grade on its 2026 infrastructure report card issued by the American Society Civil Engineers' New York State Council.
measure: ASCE state infrastructure report card New York grade

assertion: Since 2022, the rate of poor-condition bridges grew from 9.5% to 9.9%, per ASCE. The national rate was 6.7%.
sql: SELECT year, bridge_condition, COUNT(*) FROM transport.bridges WHERE record_type='1' AND state_code='36' GROUP BY year, bridge_condition
inaccuracy: ASCE's 2022 figure is about 0.3 points above the NBI count

assertion: The state has invested $18 billion in bridges in the last four years, which includes funds from the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. However, ASCE says it would take an estimated $74.5 billion to bring all of the state's bridges into good condition.

State-owned roads have improved, with excellent-condition roads growing from 17% in 2022 to 24% in 2024, according to the report card. Meanwhile, poor-condition roads owned by the state DOT decreased from 10% to 8% in the same timeframe.

Transit ridership rebounded to 85% of pre-pandemic levels on the back of New York City, which has the highest transit ridership in the nation, per ASCE. Meanwhile, transit agencies have $50 billion in state-of-good-repair investments planned over the next five years.
About 40% of the state's water pipes were installed before the 1940s. Other water systems lose up to 40% of treated water in part due to leaky pipes, per ASCE.
independent_value: 40%; up to 40%, in part due to leaky pipes (ASCE wording)

assertion: The U.S. as a whole earned a grade of 'C' in 2025, the most recent nationwide scoring.
The IIJA put $30 billion into New York projects.
A 'C-' grade indicates adequate, stable performance with the need to invest further to ensure infrastructure holds up in the future.
inaccuracy: ASCE says 'fair condition' and the overall grade fell from C; 'stable' is misleading
independent_value: ASCE: fair condition, serving adequately for now
